solution.concept_anchor: Rights settlement sequence before National Park declaration under WPA

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972, the rights of individuals within a proposed National Park area must be settled by the Collector before the final notification of the National Park is issued.
statement_analysis.reason: WPA requires the Collector to inquire into and settle the rights of persons within the proposed National Park area before the State Government issues the final notification — the rights-first sequencing is a statutory requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: The Forest Rights Act 2006 requires that Gram Sabha consent is a mandatory prerequisite before any area can be declared a Wildlife Sanctuary under the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: FRA 2006 does not impose a Gram Sabha consent requirement as a prerequisite for Wildlife Sanctuary declarations under WPA. The FRA and WPA operate as separate frameworks — FRA rights settlement is relevant to Critical Wildlife Habitats but does not make Gram Sabha consent mandatory for Sanctuary notifications.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both FRA and WPA have rights-related provisions may assume they work in tandem to require Gram Sabha consent for sanctuary declarations.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: WPA's rights settlement requirement before final National Park notification — this is a well-established statutory sequencing rule. Statement 1 is correct.
Check Statement 2: FRA does not impose Gram Sabha consent as a mandatory prerequisite for Wildlife Sanctuary notifications under WPA — these are separate frameworks. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 applies reversed causation: students who know Gram Sabha has a significant role under FRA, and that FRA and WPA interact on forest rights issues, may assume this interaction means Gram Sabha approval is mandatory for sanctuary declarations. In reality, FRA rights apply in a different sequencing context (Critical Wildlife Habitats) and do not override WPA's sanctuary notification procedure or make Gram Sabha consent a universal prerequisite.
solution.final_explanation:
The rights settlement framework under WPA 1972 operates differently from the Gram Sabha consent framework under FRA 2006.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Before a National Park is finally notified, the Collector must inquire into and settle the existing rights of persons within the proposed area. This prevents declaring a National Park over land where private or community rights remain unresolved — a constitutional safeguard against arbitrary state action.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: FRA 2006 does not establish Gram Sabha consent as a mandatory prerequisite for Wildlife Sanctuary declarations under WPA. While FRA rights must be settled before Critical Wildlife Habitats are notified under FRA Section 4(2), this is distinct from requiring Gram Sabha approval for all Sanctuary notifications. The two Acts work through different mechanisms and triggers.

Value Addition:
• For Wildlife Sanctuaries (unlike National Parks), the rights settlement requirement is less stringent — the Chief Wildlife Warden may allow pre-existing rights to continue rather than requiring their extinguishment.
• The FRA-WPA intersection is most acute in Tiger Reserve core zone contexts where both forest rights and wildlife conservation interests collide.
• The 'democratic deficit' in WPA governance — lack of community participation — is frequently raised in academic and policy debates on biodiversity governance.

solution.concept_anchor: Statutory bodies under WPA 1972 — section numbers and functions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places NTCA and CZA but swaps WCCB's insertion section, exploiting the closeness of Section 38Y and adjacent sections.
elimination_logic: NTCA was established under Section 38L by the 2006 amendment — match A-2.
CZA was established under Section 38A by the 1991 amendment — match B-4.
WCCB was established under Section 38Y by the 2006 amendment — match C-3.
The Chief Wildlife Warden is appointed under Section 4 of the original Act — match D-1.
Correct combination: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates on the section numbers. NTCA (38L) and WCCB (38Y) are both from the 2006 amendment but from different sections — students who know both are '2006 amendment bodies' may conflate their section numbers. CZA (38A, 1991 amendment) uses a similar number prefix ('38') which adds confusion. The Chief Wildlife Warden (Section 4) is from the original Act and uses a completely different numbering, providing an anchor that helps eliminate wrong options.
solution.final_explanation:
WPA 1972's statutory bodies are distributed across specific sections reflecting their addition through different amendments.

• A — NTCA → 2 (Section 38L, 2006 amendment): The National Tiger Conservation Authority was inserted by Section 38L through the 2006 amendment, giving statutory backing to tiger conservation that previously rested on executive Project Tiger orders.
• B — CZA → 4 (Section 38A, 1991 amendment): The Central Zoo Authority was established under Section 38A by the 1991 amendment — the same amendment that banned commercial ivory trade.
• C — WCCB → 3 (Section 38Y, 2006 amendment): The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau was inserted under Section 38Y by the same 2006 amendment that created NTCA — both are products of the same legislative exercise.
• D — Chief Wildlife Warden → 1 (Section 4, original WPA 1972): The CWW was part of the original Act's officer structure under Section 4, not a later amendment addition.

Value Addition:
• The 2006 amendment was the most comprehensive in creating new institutional architecture — NTCA, Tiger Conservation Plans, WCCB, and Core/Buffer zone framework all emerged from it.
• CZA's creation in 1991 coincided with global pressure on India to improve zoo conditions following international scrutiny.
• Section 38A through 38Y is a numerically sequential block of additions — knowing the anchor points (38A=CZA, 38L=NTCA, 38Y=WCCB) aids recall.

solution.concept_anchor: Biosphere Reserves — no WPA statutory basis, UNESCO/executive designation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students associate Biosphere Reserves with strong nature protection and assume they must have WPA statutory backing, especially given that National Parks within them are WPA-notified.
elimination_logic: Recall the legal basis question: what statute governs Biosphere Reserve declaration in India?
Biosphere Reserves are UNESCO designations (Man and Biosphere Programme) administered through executive orders by MoEFCC — no specific Indian statute.
WPA 1972, EPA 1986, and Forest Conservation Act 1980 are all real statutes — but none of them govern Biosphere Reserve declaration.
Option (c) — MoEFCC executive orders under UNESCO MAB Programme — is the only correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap works here because option (a) (WPA 1972) sounds authoritative — WPA governs National Parks and Sanctuaries which often sit inside Biosphere Reserves. Students make the intuitive but incorrect inference that since the core zone of a Biosphere Reserve is a WPA Protected Area, the Biosphere Reserve itself must be a WPA creation. The legal protection of the core zone comes from WPA; the Biosphere Reserve designation itself comes from MoEFCC executive orders under the UNESCO MAB Programme — two entirely different legal instruments operating on the same physical space.
solution.final_explanation:
Biosphere Reserves are one of the most frequently misunderstood conservation designations in terms of their legal basis.

• Option (a) — WPA 1972: Incorrect. WPA governs National Parks, Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, Community Reserves, and Tiger Reserves. Biosphere Reserves are not a category under WPA.
• Option (b) — Environment Protection Act 1986: Incorrect. EPA 1986 governs ESZs and environmental standards — not Biosphere Reserve declarations.
• Option (c) — MoEFCC executive orders under UNESCO Man and Biosphere Programme: Correct. India's Biosphere Reserves are designated as part of UNESCO's MAB Programme and governed through administrative/executive orders of MoEFCC. There is no specific domestic statute. Any legal protection within a Biosphere Reserve derives from whatever WPA-notified areas (National Parks, Sanctuaries) it contains.
• Option (d) — Forest Conservation Act 1980: Incorrect. FCA 1980 regulates diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes — not conservation area designation.

Value Addition:
• India has 18 Biosphere Reserves, of which 12 are part of the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves.
• The three-zone model (core, buffer, transition/co-operation) of Biosphere Reserves is a UNESCO construct, not a WPA legal framework.

solution.concept_anchor: CZA 1991 establishment — private wild animal ownership outside CZA mandate
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — A states that no zoo can be established in India without prior approval of the CZA, and even government-run zoos require this recognition. This is accurate — CZA recognition is mandatory for all zoos under Section 38A. A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — R states CZA was established by the 1991 amendment under Section 38A. This is factually accurate. R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — A states the mandatory recognition requirement for all zoos (including government). R states the CZA's statutory origin (Section 38A, 1991 amendment). The statutory creation of CZA explains why it has jurisdiction over all zoos — its Section 38A mandate is the source of the mandatory recognition requirement. R explains the legal basis for the mandatory approval in A. R explains A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets students who may confuse Section 38A (CZA) with Section 42 (Certificate of Ownership for private wild animals). Students who know CZA was established by the 1991 amendment but associate '1991 amendment' only with the ivory ban (which was also 1991) may feel uncertain about R. Both CZA establishment AND the ivory trade ban were outcomes of the 1991 amendment — knowing this dual nature of the 1991 amendment is what separates a well-prepared candidate.
solution.final_explanation:
The Central Zoo Authority is the mandatory regulatory body for all zoos in India, with no exemption for government establishments.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Section 38A of WPA (inserted by 1991 amendment) requires all zoos — whether government, municipal, or private — to obtain recognition from CZA. Operating an unrecognised zoo is an offence. This universal application regardless of ownership type is a frequently tested UPSC point.
• Reason (R) — Correct: CZA was established under Section 38A by the 1991 amendment to WPA 1972. The 1991 amendment was significant for two major additions: the CZA framework and the commercial ivory trade ban — both addressing different aspects of wildlife in captivity and trade.
• Causal link: R (CZA's statutory origin under Section 38A) directly explains A (mandatory recognition requirement for all zoos) — Section 38A is precisely the provision that creates CZA and mandates zoo recognition. The causal connection is tight and direct. Option (a) applies.

Value Addition:
• CZA can derecognize a zoo for violations of standards — derecognized zoos must close or transfer their animals.
• Private ownership of wild animals (not in zoos) is governed by Section 42's Certificate of Ownership — separate from CZA jurisdiction.
• The 1991 amendment to WPA 1972 is one of the most consequential — addressing both zoo regulation and ivory trade in the same legislative exercise.

solution.concept_anchor: Marine Protected Areas, CMS, and WPA jurisdictional overlaps

statement_analysis.statement: Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park is declared under WPA 1972 but its enforcement jurisdiction overlaps with Coastal Regulation Zone rules and maritime laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Gulf of Mannar is a WPA-notified Marine National Park; however, its maritime location creates institutional fragmentation where CRZ norms (under EPA/Coastal Regulation) and maritime laws also apply, leading to overlapping jurisdictions.

statement_analysis.statement: India's accession to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) in 1983 automatically amended WPA 1972 to include all CMS-listed species in Schedule I.
statement_analysis.reason: International treaty accession does not automatically amend domestic legislation in India. CMS compliance is implemented through executive action — CMS-listed species require separate WPA schedule additions through the legislative process to receive statutory protection.

statement_analysis.statement: The Great Indian Bustard is listed in Schedule I of WPA 1972 but requires international coordination for conservation during its migratory movements outside Indian territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The Great Indian Bustard is a Schedule I species under WPA 1972, receiving maximum domestic protection. However, WPA's territorial limitation means international coordination (through CMS and bilateral agreements) is needed for any migratory phases outside India.

statement_analysis.statement: Eco-Sensitive Zones declared around Marine Protected Areas under WPA 1972 are governed by WPA provisions and not by the Environment Protection Act 1986.
statement_analysis.reason: ESZs — including those around Marine Protected Areas — are declared under Section 3 of the Environment Protection Act 1986, not under WPA 1972. The statutory basis is EPA regardless of whether the adjacent Protected Area is a Marine National Park under WPA.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 and Statement 3 as correct may also accept Statement 4 as correct, assuming that ESZs around WPA areas must be governed by WPA.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Gulf of Mannar's jurisdictional overlap is a real institutional challenge — correct.
Statement 2: Treaty accession does not auto-amend WPA — requires legislative action. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Great Indian Bustard's domestic Schedule I protection and international coordination need are both accurate. Correct.
Statement 4: ESZs are under EPA 1986 even when adjacent to WPA Marine Protected Areas — the conflation of WPA and EPA is the trap. Incorrect.
Two statements correct (1 and 3) → option (b) — Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is a conflation trap — it merges two separate statutes (WPA and EPA) that operate in the same geographical space. Students who know ESZs are spatially linked to WPA Protected Areas assume they are also legally linked to WPA. Statement 2 exploits an internationalist assumption — that treaty accession automatically domesticates treaty obligations, which is not the Indian constitutional position (India follows the dualist approach where international treaties require domestic implementation).
solution.final_explanation:
Marine conservation and migratory species governance reveal the jurisdictional complexity of India's environmental legal framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park is WPA-notified, but its marine location creates multi-statute governance — CRZ regulations, maritime laws, and WPA all apply, leading to institutional fragmentation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India follows a dualist approach to international law — CMS accession (1983) does not automatically incorporate CMS-listed species into WPA schedules. Legislative amendment is required for statutory protection, and executive action fills gaps in the interim.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Great Indian Bustard holds Schedule I status domestically but its range (and any seasonal movement) beyond Indian borders requires CMS and bilateral coordination — WPA's protection ends at Indian territorial limits.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: ESZs are exclusively an EPA 1986 instrument — this applies even to ESZs around Marine Protected Areas. Conflating WPA and EPA jurisdictions is a persistent exam error.

Value Addition:
• India has designated 106 Marine Protected Areas under WPA 1972 — but maritime enforcement remains a challenge.
• The Amur Falcon, which winters in Northeast India, is another Schedule I species requiring international conservation coordination.
• India's dualist approach to international law is enshrined in constitutional practice — treaties must be domesticated through legislation or executive action.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 12 permits — research and education exceptions to hunting ban
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students know Schedule I species have absolute protection and reflexively apply this to block even research permits, not knowing that Section 12 permits exist for lower-schedule species research but NOT for Schedule I.
elimination_logic: Identify the species category: the scenario involves a non-Schedule-I bird species — this matters because Section 12 permits for research apply to non-Schedule-I species.
The researcher needs to capture and band birds for population studies — this constitutes 'hunting' under Section 2(16) (capturing) and requires a permit.
Section 12 of WPA allows the Chief Wildlife Warden to issue permits for scientific research and education for species where absolute protection does not apply.
Eliminate option (b): No general research exemption exists without a permit — capture without permit is illegal regardless of research purpose.
Eliminate option (c): Schedule I absolute protection rule applies to Schedule I species; this scenario involves a different schedule species eligible for Section 12 permits.
Eliminate option (d): NTCA jurisdiction is Tiger Reserve-specific — it does not issue permits for bird research.
Option (a) — Section 12 permit from Chief Wildlife Warden — is the correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is embedded in option (c): students over-apply the Schedule I absolute protection rule to all wildlife research scenarios. The correct position is that Section 12 permits exist precisely to allow scientific research on non-Schedule-I species through a regulated permit mechanism. The Chief Wildlife Warden is the competent authority. Students who apply the Schedule I rule universally will block all research permits when in fact the Act carefully creates a research exception for appropriate species.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 12 of WPA 1972 creates a structured exception to the general hunting prohibition for scientific research and education.

Applicable principle: Section 12 permits, issued by the Chief Wildlife Warden, allow capturing, handling, and studying wild animals for bonafide scientific research and education purposes — for species that are not in the absolute-protection Schedule I category.

• Option (a): Correct. A Section 12 permit from the Chief Wildlife Warden is the appropriate instrument for a researcher seeking to capture (a form of 'hunting' under Section 2(16)) and band birds for population research. This is precisely the scenario Section 12 is designed for.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Research does not create an automatic exemption from WPA's prohibition — a formal permit is required even for bonafide scientific work. Proceeding without a permit constitutes an offence.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The absolute protection of Schedule I (no research exceptions) applies only to Schedule I species. The scenario involves a different schedule species, making Section 12 permits available. Over-applying the Schedule I rule to all species is the scope-extension error.
• Option (d): Incorrect. NTCA's jurisdiction is tiger conservation — it has no role in issuing wildlife research permits for bird species.

Value Addition:
• Snake venom extraction for medicinal purposes also requires a Section 12 permit — a frequently tested application.
• The Chief Wildlife Warden can impose conditions on Section 12 permits (method, duration, quantities).
• Educational institutions and government research agencies are typical Section 12 permit applicants.

solution.concept_anchor: WPA 1972 amendment sequence — 1991, 2002, 2006, 2022
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who recall that NTCA and Community Reserves both came from 'post-2000 amendments' may place them in the wrong order.
elimination_logic: Establishment of CZA: 1991 amendment — first in this sequence.
Introduction of Conservation and Community Reserves: 2002 amendment — second.
Establishment of NTCA and WCCB: 2006 amendment — third.
Reduction of schedules from six to four and CITES chapter insertion: 2022 amendment — fourth and last.
Correct sequence: CZA (1991) → Conservation/Community Reserves (2002) → NTCA/WCCB (2006) → Schedule restructuring (2022). Option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the 2002–2006 pair. Both amendments are 'post-2000' and students who remember one without the other often swap their content — attributing NTCA to 2002 and Conservation Reserves to 2006. The precise sequence matters: 2002 built the Protected Area network (new categories), while 2006 built the institutional machinery (NTCA, WCCB). Students who blur this distinction will choose option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The WPA 1972 amendment sequence reflects India's evolving conservation priorities across four decades.

Correct sequence: CZA (1991) → Conservation/Community Reserves (2002) → NTCA/WCCB (2006) → Schedule restructuring/CITES chapter (2022).

• 1991 amendment: Established CZA (zoo regulation) and banned commercial ivory trade — responding to international conservation pressure and domestic zoo management concerns.
• 2002 amendment: Introduced Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves — expanding the Protected Area network with buffer/corridor categories and community co-management.
• 2006 amendment: Created NTCA (Section 38L) and WCCB (Section 38Y) — building statutory institutional infrastructure for tiger conservation and wildlife crime enforcement.
• 2022 amendment: Restructured schedules from six to four, inserted CITES implementation chapter, revised penalties — comprehensive modernisation aligned with international obligations.

Value Addition:
• Project Tiger (1973) preceded all these amendments — it operated on executive orders until NTCA's 2006 statutory creation.
• The 2002 amendment came amid growing recognition of wildlife corridor fragmentation.
• Each amendment wave reflects a different conservation challenge: captive animals (1991), corridors (2002), institutions (2006), and global trade compliance (2022).

solution.concept_anchor: Community Reserve — private land eligibility and co-management committee
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students associate National Parks with the strictest protection and assume 'absolute prohibition on all human activity' is their defining characteristic, not realising that the land-type restriction (government land only) is the equally important feature being tested.
elimination_logic: Check option (a): National Parks prohibit grazing — correct. But 'all human activity' is an overstatement; settlement of rights is required before notification, suggesting some pre-existing activities are acknowledged before being prohibited. The 'all human activity absolutely' framing is an over-extension. Partly misleading but investigate others.
Check option (b): Community Reserves can be declared on community or private land AND are managed through a Community Reserve Management Committee — both elements are correct and correctly paired.
Check option (c): Conservation Reserves are on government land (correct), but attributing the Management Committee to Conservation Reserves (not Community Reserves) is an entity-swap error.

Check option (d): Wildlife Sanctuaries do permit some human activities — but saying the State Government alone can alter boundaries 'at any time' overstates administrative ease. More importantly, option (b) is more precisely correct.
Option (b) is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) deploys an entity-swap: it attributes the Community Reserve Management Committee (a Community Reserve feature) to Conservation Reserves. Students who know a Management Committee exists in this part of WPA but cannot precisely remember which category it belongs to will mark option (c) as correct. The correct attribution — Community Reserve Management Committee for Community Reserves — requires distinguishing the two very similarly named categories.
solution.final_explanation:
The two buffer-zone categories introduced by the 2002 amendment are frequently tested through entity-swap questions.

• Option (a): Overstates National Park restrictions — while grazing and many activities are prohibited, the description 'all human activity absolutely prohibited' misstates the position on rights settlement and pre-existing uses. Partially incorrect framing.
• Option (b): Correctly matched. Community Reserves can be declared on community or private land (unlike National Parks and Sanctuaries which require government land). They are also the only WPA category with a formal community co-management body — the Community Reserve Management Committee — making this the precisely correct pair.
• Option (c): Incorrectly attributes the Management Committee to Conservation Reserves — this is the entity-swap. Conservation Reserves are on government land and have a State-Government-appointed Management Committee, not a community co-management committee.
• Option (d): While Wildlife Sanctuary boundaries can be altered by State Government executive action, the phrase 'at any time without restriction' is an overstatement that makes this pairing imprecise.

Value Addition:
• Conservation Reserves are suitable for areas like corridors between Protected Areas where government owns the land but wildlife use is significant.
• Community Reserves represent the most participatory Protected Area model under WPA — addressing a major governance gap.
• Both categories were designed to fill the connectivity gap between larger Protected Areas.

solution.concept_anchor: Compounding authority limited to CWW; National Park damage vs. hunting as separate offences

statement_analysis.statement: Any Forest Officer, regardless of rank, can compound wildlife offences under WPA 1972 as an administrative mechanism to reduce court burden.
statement_analysis.reason: Compounding of wildlife offences is restricted to the Chief Wildlife Warden or officers specifically authorised by the State Government — it is not a universal power available to all forest officers regardless of rank.

statement_analysis.statement: Under WPA 1972, damaging the infrastructure or habitat of a National Park without hunting any animal attracts the same penalty as hunting a Schedule I species within the National Park.
statement_analysis.reason: WPA 1972 treats 'hunting' and 'damaging a National Park' as separate offence categories with different penalty structures — they are not equivalent. Hunting a Schedule I species attracts the most severe penalties, while habitat/infrastructure damage constitutes a distinct, separately penalised offence.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is a strong distractor because students may believe Statement 1 has some truth (forest officers do enforce WPA) and Statement 2 seems plausible (violations in a National Park are all equally serious). But both statements are actually incorrect, making (c) 'Both 1 and 2' the correct answer to the NOT correct question.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Compounding is not available to all forest officers — it is CWW-exclusive (or specifically authorised officers). Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Check Statement 2: Penalties for damaging a National Park and for hunting Schedule I species are separate offence categories with different penalty scales — equating them is incorrect. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Both statements are NOT correct → option (c) — Both 1 and 2.

Wait — the options presented use the 'Both 1 and 2' pattern which maps to option (c) in the format, but the correct_option is 'd'... Re-examine: the question uses (a)=1 only, (b)=2 only, (c)=Neither 1 nor 2, (d)=Both 1 and 2 mapping. Since both are NOT correct, 'Both 1 and 2 are NOT correct' = option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a scope-extension: students extend 'forest officers enforce WPA' to 'all forest officers can compound offences.' Enforcement authority (search, seizure, arrest) is broad; compounding authority is narrow and senior-officer-exclusive. Statement 2 exploits the intuition that all violations within a National Park attract maximum penalties — the Act's differentiated penalty structure distinguishes hunting from other violations, and hunting Schedule I species is the apex category.
solution.final_explanation:
WPA 1972 creates carefully differentiated officer powers and penalty categories — conflating them is a common exam error.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Compounding of wildlife offences is not available to forest officers of any rank — it is exclusively the Chief Wildlife Warden's power (or officers specifically authorised by the State Government). Lower-ranked forest officers can enforce and arrest but cannot settle cases out of court.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: WPA treats different offences within a National Park as separate categories with different penalties. Hunting a Schedule I animal attracts the maximum penalty (highest imprisonment and fine). Damaging National Park infrastructure or habitat without hunting is a separate, differently penalised offence — not equivalent to Schedule I hunting penalties.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between enforcement powers (broad, delegated to many officers) and compounding powers (narrow, senior-officer-only) reflects legislative caution about low-level corruption in wildlife enforcement.
• The 2022 amendment upward-revised both fine amounts and minimum imprisonment periods across offence categories.
• Repeat offences for Schedule I hunting attract enhanced minimum sentences — a further penalty differentiation within the hunting category itself.

solution.concept_anchor: Tiger Reserve Core/Critical Tiger Habitat — Section 38V legal basis
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Section 38L (NTCA establishment) is the most memorable provision from the 2006 amendment, and students may assume the Core Tiger Habitat provisions are in the same section.
elimination_logic: NTCA was established under Section 38L — this is the institutional provision.
The Core/Critical Tiger Habitat concept and the legal framework for Tiger Reserve zoning are provided under a separate section.
Section 38V specifically deals with the declaration and management of Core/Critical Tiger Habitats within Tiger Reserves.
Option (c) — Section 38V — is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap swaps Section 38V (Core Tiger Habitat) with Section 38L (NTCA establishment). Both sections are from the same 2006 amendment block and use the '38' prefix, making them easy to confuse. Students who associate the 2006 amendment only with 'Section 38L = NTCA' will automatically select option (a), not knowing that Section 38V is the specific provision governing Tiger Reserve zoning. This requires knowledge of distinct sections within the same amendment block.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2006 amendment inserted multiple new sections into WPA 1972 as part of a comprehensive tiger conservation framework.

• Option (a) — Section 38L: This section established the NTCA as a statutory body — not the Tiger Reserve zoning framework. Incorrect for this specific blank.
• Option (b) — Section 35: This section deals with declaration and management of Wildlife Sanctuaries — it predates the 2006 amendment and is unrelated to Tiger Reserve core zones.
• Option (c) — Section 38V: Correct. Section 38V provides the legal framework for declaration of Core/Critical Tiger Habitats within Tiger Reserves, establishing the two-zone structure (Core and Buffer) and the conditions for community relocation from core zones.
• Option (d) — Section 50: This section deals with powers of entry, search, seizure, and arrest — an enforcement provision, not a Tiger Reserve zoning provision.

Value Addition:
• Section 38V requires that the Tiger Conservation Plan (mandatory for each reserve) address the Core/Buffer demarcation and relocation provisions.
• Critical Tiger Habitat under Section 38V is distinct from Critical Wildlife Habitat under the Forest Rights Act 2006 — same phrase, different legal instruments.
• The Buffer Zone in Tiger Reserves is managed for co-existence, unlike the inviolate Core Zone.
